translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil on the martyr Julitta, and on what was lacking in the previously delivered chapter, and also on thanksgiving
This gathering of the church is for the preaching concerning the holy martyr, for we announced this day to you,
on which falls the commemoration of her great struggle, which she carried out in her woman's nature bravely and in a way astonishing to the mind of all,
both those who beheld her at that time and those who heard of it afterward: the blessed one among women, Julitta.
And is it even right to call her a woman, who by the strength and courage of her mind covered over the weakness of women's nature?
By her the enemy of us all was wounded all the more, for he could not bear this defeat of his at the hands of women,
he who was greatly arrogant and boasted that he would shake the whole earth and seize it
like a bird's [?] nest, and that he would take up and lay waste mighty cities and the whole world like abandoned eggs. Such a one was found defeated by the virtue of a woman and a tender child,
whose weakness he set about exposing at the time of trial, for he supposed
that because of her weak nature she would be unable to keep her faith in her God to the end.
But when he put her to the test, he found her stronger than that nature, and his arrogance was rebuked by her as greatly as he had imagined he would rebuke her.
For she had a lawsuit with a certain man among the powerful of that city, a greedy man and an oppressor, who had acquired his wealth by robbery,

and who had seized from the blessed woman much land, and her estates, slaves, and flocks, and the rest of her property. He had come to the court trusting in bringing false witnesses and winning by bribes.
But when the lady came forward, and the herald was crying out, and the advocates were ready, the blessed woman wished to speak about that man's oppression,
and about how she had acquired that property from the first, and about the length of time during which she had held it, which confirmed her ownership.
And then she wished to speak of his oppression, how he had seized all of it from her.
Then her legal opponent came forward and said: "This trial is not proper, for it is not right for justice to be received among us by one
who does not serve the gods and the command of the emperors, but holds the faith of Christ."
The ruler heard this and reckoned the argument just, and at once tortures were prepared, fire and sword, so that if she denied Christ, justice and her property would be given to her;
but if she kept the faith, not only would justice not be given to her, but not even life, as one who insulted the emperors.
But behold what she did! Did wealth perhaps lead her astray? Or out of rivalry with her opponent did she despise what is better?
Or was she frightened by the tortures? God forbid! Rather she cried out: "Let this life go, let all my property perish,
let my body not remain upon me, rather than that I should speak any lawless word concerning my Creator."
And the more she saw the ruler turning savage at these words and inflamed to the utmost wrath,
So much the more did she give thanks to God, for in contending for corruptible possessions she was shown to be one who gained those good things that do not pass away.
And the land was being taken from her so that paradise might be given to her; and she endured insult, which brings about that incorruptible crown;
and she was beaten in the flesh, and this passing life was being taken from her, for the hope of that heavenly blessedness and so that she might enter the kingdom of heaven with all the saints.
And as they questioned her many times, and she many times gave them the same answer, confessing herself a handmaid of Christ and cursing those
who were calling on her to deny him, then that judge of lawlessness not only
took from her those possessions, unjustly seized, but also gave her herself over to the fire and, as he supposed, banished her from life.
But she had never gone toward the beautiful things of this world with such joy and at such a run
as she went toward that flame, with a radiant face and a look of joy; and by the words
that she spoke she showed forth the joy of her soul, and she implored the women standing there
not to become faint-hearted toward the labors and contests of piety, and not to plead natural weakness as an excuse.
For she said to them: "We too are of the same nature as men; we were created in the image of God, just as they were.
Women too are capable of receiving virtue, and in honor they were created by God equal to man.
For what difference is there between us and their nature?
For not only flesh was taken for the creation of woman, but also bone from his bones; and therefore courage and firmness and endurance are required of us just as of men."
She said this and ran toward the fire. And the furnace received the body of that saint
as a bridal chamber of light, and it sent up her soul to that heavenly world and that longed-for rest.
But it preserved that precious body unharmed; it lies in the beautiful church before the city, and it sanctifies that place and sanctifies those who enter there.
And the ground, which was blessed by the laying there of that blessed one, sent up from its depths beautiful water, for the martyr, like a mother with milk, suckles that city.
This water is a guardian of the healthy, a giver of greater delight to those who take their delight rightly and with the fear of God, and a consolation for the sick.

For the grace that Elisha bestowed on the people of Jericho, this martyr has graciously given to us: by her blessing she changed the salty nature of the waters of that place into sweetness and pleasantness.
But, O men, do not consent to be inferior to women in piety;
O women, do not fall away from this example, but keep the true faith without excuse, since you have been amply proven by deed:
the deficiency of your nature can keep you from none of the good things.
I very much wished to speak about this martyr, but the discourse we began yesterday, which remained incomplete, did not allow me to say many words for this day.
For I am by nature burdened by every unfinished work, just as an image [left unfinished] is unsightly.
...portrayed only halfway; and the road is useless to travelers if they do not reach the place toward which they set out,
and so too with the business of hunting: when the hunter toils greatly and comes close to catching the game, yet catches it nowhere,
his labor proves useless; and those who run in the stadium are often left behind by a single step and shut out from the crown.
So we too yesterday brought up those words of the Apostle and thought that we could go through their meaning in a few short words,
but we have found that what was left out is greater than what was said; therefore it seems right to me to complete what was lacking.
For the Apostle said: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything."
Now concerning rejoicing always, we spoke on that first day, though not as was fitting, but according to our ability.
But concerning unceasing prayer, and whether it is possible to fulfill that commandment, you too,
you who ask, are ready, and I too, according to my ability, will answer you and carry out this service of the word.
For prayer is a request for good, which believers make to God.
But we do not make that request in words, for we do not suppose that God needed to be reminded by words; rather, he knows every good thing even without our asking.
What then am I saying? Or what is my argument? That we need to accomplish prayer not by words,
but rather by the mind of the soul and by works of virtue, with which our life should be adorned, as it has been said:
"Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything to the glory of God."
And when you sit at table, pray; when you take bread, offer thanks to the one who gives it; and again,
when you comfort the weakness of the body with wine, remember him who gives wine to gladden the heart and to comfort weakness.
And when the need for eating has passed, let the remembrance of the Benefactor not depart.
When you put on a tunic, thank the one who gives it; when you put on a garment, increase your love toward God,
who has given us clothing suited to both winter and summer, which preserves our life and covers what is unseemly.
And when the day ends, give thanks to him who has granted us the sun for use in the works of the day, and who has also given fire to give light at night and to serve readily for other needs.
And again, the night would give you other reasons for thanksgiving: when you look up to heaven and gaze on the beauty of the stars,
pray to the King of all and worship God, the skillful Creator of all, who made everything in wisdom.
And again, when you see the whole nature of living creatures seized by sleep, worship him who, without our willing it,
gives us rest from the labors of the day through sleep and, by that brief rest, brings us back again to the vigor of our strength.
And therefore let not the whole night be the portion of sleep alone, nor allow half of your life to be useless through the unconsciousness of sleep.
But let the time of night be divided for you between sleep and prayer.
And let your very sleep be an exercise of piety, for the fancies of sleep arise for the most part from the exercises of the day:
for as the deeds of our life are, such for the most part do our dreams become in sleep as well.
And if your life is like this, then you pray without ceasing, for you do not accomplish prayer by word alone,
but by the whole conduct of your life you have joined yourself to God, and your whole life is a united and unceasing prayer.
Hear, then, also that other saying of the Apostle: "In everything give thanks."
But someone may say: "And how can a soul do this when it is gripped by trials and afflicted,
when it is pierced as if by a goad by the memory of those distressing things?
And how could it not lament and weep, but instead give thanks, as if for something good, for what are truly evils?
For if my enemy strikes me and these things come upon me, how can I give thanks for them?
When death has snatched away my child before his time, and pains worse than the former ones
come upon the parents because of their beloved one, how then shall I leave off mourning over this and begin to give thanks?" How?
Listen, and I will tell you: if you consider and understand that God the Father is closer to the one born of you, and is a wiser protector and governor of life.
Why then do we not allow his own creatures to be governed as the wise King wills?
But it is grievous to us, as though something of ours were being taken from us, and we pity the dead as though some injustice had befallen them.
But you should understand it this way: the child has not died but has been given over to God; nor has the friend come to an end,
but he has departed and has gone on a little ahead on the road that we too must undoubtedly travel.
Let the commandment of God dwell with you, which will give you light and understanding to discern these matters,

which will take hold of the thought of your soul from afar, and give you a worthy and true understanding of each matter, and prepare you, and not allow you to change your mind because of even one of the things that befall you,
but rather, with a mind prepared from the beginning, you may be like a rock near the sea and bear unshaken the onset of fierce winds and waves.
For why did you not accustom yourself from the beginning to reflect on the mortality of that mortal one, instead of receiving the child's death as something unexpected?
When the birth of that child was first announced to you, if someone had asked you what sort of being the newborn was, what would you have answered?
Would you have answered anything other than this, that it was a human being? But if it was a human being, it is evident that it was also mortal.
What is so astonishing, then, if the mortal one has died? Do you not see the sun, how it rises and sets again?
Do you not see the moon, how it waxes and then wanes? Do you not see the earth, how it flourishes and then withers?
What among our affairs is firm? What thing has a nature that is unshakable and unchangeable?
Look up to heaven and look down at the earth, for not even these are eternal, as it is written:
"Heaven and earth will pass away, and the stars will fall from heaven, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light."
What wonder is it, then, if we too, since we are parts of the world, become sharers in the affairs of the world?
Consider all this, and when the portion of these things that are common to all comes upon you as well,
lower your eyes and bear it, not without pain and without feeling (for what merit would there be in insensibility?), but with great pain and manifold anguish.
Yet endure, like a brave soldier who shows his strength and courage not only by striking his opponents and wounding them,
but also by bearing the blows and wounds they deal him; and like a skilled ship's master, wise and unperturbed,
whose great experience keeps his soul unperturbed in the time of trials and waves and of the great storm.
For the loss of a beloved child, or of a spouse, or of any others among those he loves, will not seem at all an evil to the one
who has been prepared from the first, and who has right reason as the overseer and ruler of his life, and who does not walk merely according to the flesh,
for separation from what they are accustomed to seems hard even to beasts.
And I once saw an ox weeping over the death of its yoke-mate, and other beasts too bear heavily the loss of what they are accustomed to.

But this is not what you have learned, nor is this what has been preached to you. Rather, the beginning of love arises from much being together and from the habit of long years, and this is not unfitting,
nor is it evil; but lamenting over separation is altogether beastlike.
Suppose a spouse has been joined to you, who brought you joy and was a helper in life,
a sharer in joy and a fellow mourner in sorrow, and such a one is snatched away by death in an instant:
do not become foolish through that passion, and do not imagine that any of our affairs is ungoverned, as if there were no governor of the world.
Do not call him a doer of evil through that excess of rejoicing [?], nor devise evil thoughts, nor stray outside the bounds of right belief.
For since the two of you became one flesh, it is a matter of great distress for the one who receives with pain the sundering of that union.
But it is not right for this reason to imagine or say anything improper, for understand that God, who created us and gave us souls,
gave each soul its own task, and set for one person one limit of this life and for another person another.
For he ordained that one should remain long in this flesh, and he commanded that another be released early from these bonds of the flesh, by that ineffable word of his wisdom and justice.
For just as with those who are placed in prisons, some remain a long time in the afflictions of prison, and others soon find release from affliction there,
Likewise some souls are held more tightly captive in this life and some less, according to the worth of each,
just as our Creator arranges for each one, wisely and profoundly, for human nature cannot reach the depth of his providence.
Have you not heard David, how he says: "Bring my soul out of prison"?
Have you not heard about that holy man of whom it is written: "His soul was released"?
And again Simeon, when he took our Lord in his arms, what did he say? Did he not say this: "Now release your servant, Lord"?
For to one who is hastening to the heavenly dwelling-place, being in this flesh is heavier than any torment and any prison.
Do not, then, seek that those dispensations concerning souls should be as you find comforting and as you wish.
Rather, understand those who are joined together in this world and afterwards are parted by death in this way: they are like travellers,
who were going along one road and, through being together, become attached to one another by habit, and who, when they have completed that shared road and come to the parting of the ways,
where the needs of their business separate each from the other, do not sit down on account of that habit of being together and neglect what lies before them,
but they remember the reason for which they set out in the first place, and each hastens to his own business.
And just as the purpose of their journey was a different one, and their union with one another happened along the road, so also are those
who have been united in this life, whether through children and parenthood, or through some other fellowship of this passing world.
And it is clear that the end of each one's life lay ahead when their union came about,
but that time of the end, which had been appointed from the beginning, separated them and dissolved their unity.
But one who has a good mind does not foolishly find that separation strange and evil, but gives thanks to the one who joined them for that original union.
But you, when there was with you a spouse, or a child, or a friend, or whoever it is for whom you now mourn, did not give thanks to the Giver, but grieved for want of more:
if you had only a spouse, why had children not also been given to you; and if there were children, why were you not very rich, or why did you see one of your enemies prospering.
Now consider: perhaps we ourselves bring about the taking of those loved ones from us:
when they were with us, we were not thankful to God, but when he has taken them away, then we grieve; for since, for the good things of God
given to us, we do not give thanks, therefore they are justly taken from us, so that we may recognize what had been given to us.
For just as the eyes cannot see things very close to them and lying right upon them, but need some small distance,
so are the souls of the ungrateful; for when they have become estranged from the good thing that was given, after its departure they recognize that grace;
for when they had it in their hands, they offered not one word of thanks to the Giver, and after being deprived of it, they call blessed what is past.
But there is not one of us who could not give thanks to God for the coming of trials, if only he is willing to understand these matters with a right mind.
For the life of each person holds many things, and not insignificant ones, for which he may give thanks to God.
If we are willing to look toward those lower than ourselves, then, when we find people more afflicted than we are, we will understand in what good circumstances we are.
For if you are a slave and there is another lower than you, give thanks that you are above at least one person, for you are not the lowest of all, with blows always coming down on you.
And again, let him who is lower than all and endures beatings give thanks as well, because he is not bound in prison and his feet are not in the stocks.
Again, let him who is in prison and in bonds not lack reasons for thanksgiving either,
for he has this life, which is enough to give thanks for: he sees the sun, he breathes the air; let him give thanks for this.
Again, if you are suffering unjustly, rejoice in the hope of the good things to come; but if you are suffering justly,
even so give thanks to God, because you are receiving the punishment for those sins here and now, and you are not being reserved for eternal judgment for all your sins.
And in this way it is right, in all the matters of this life, to give great thanks to God for his goodness.
But as it is, many are ungrateful: they despise what has been given to them and long for what they do not have, for they do not take account of those lower than themselves,

so as to give thanks in this way to the Benefactor for what has been given to them; instead they look at those higher than themselves and dwell on their own lack, as though someone had taken away what was theirs.
So they grieve over the possessions and glory of others, and so they are ungrateful and full of accusation:
the slave grieves because he is not a nobleman; the one who was raised in freedom grieves that he is not from rich parents,
because he does not have ancestors he could count up to seven generations of grandfathers, who would have spent their days in governorships and high honors;
again, the one who is from distinguished parents grieves because he is not filled with great wealth;
the rich man grieves because he is not lord of cities and nations; the governor, because he is not king;
the king is ungrateful because he does not hold the whole earth, but there are nations somewhere that do not obey his command.
And from all this it comes about that the Benefactor is thanked for nothing.
But let us give up grieving over things of no substance, and let us learn to give thanks for what has been given to us.
When we are in afflictions and trial, let us say to that all-wise Physician:
"Your instruction upon us is a small affliction." Let us say: "It is good for me that you have humbled me."
Let us say: "The sufferings of this age are not worthy of the eternal glory that is to be revealed upon us."
Let us say: "These torments and afflictions are small compared with our sins."
Let us entreat the Lord and say: "Instruct us, Lord, but with justice and not in anger," for:
"If we are judged, we are disciplined by God, so that we may not be condemned along with the world."
But when we are in rest and prosperity, then let us say that word of David: "What shall I repay the Lord for all this that he has repaid me?
" For he brought us from non-being into being, honored us with speech, and graciously gave us the arts as helpers of our life.
He makes food spring up from the earth, and he has given us the service and use of green plants.
For us are the rains, for us is the sun; the mountains and plains have been made for us, so that we may dwell wherever we wish.
For us the rivers flow, for us the springs have welled up.
The sea has been given to us to travel on, along with the riches that come up from the earth and comforts of every kind.
All creation serves us because of the ungrudging grace of our Creator, which he has poured out upon us.
And why is there any need to speak of these lowly matters?
I will speak of those lofty matters: for our sake God came among men, and for the sake of corrupted flesh "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" - the Benefactor among the ungrateful.
To captives came the Liberator, to those sitting in darkness, the "Sun of righteousness."
The impassible one was lifted up on the cross, Life went to death, the Light descended into hell, he who is the resurrection for the fallen.
He has granted us the Spirit of adoption, the distributions of graces, the promises of crowns, and his other good gifts, which are impossible to enumerate,
on account of which the word of the prophet is fitting: "What shall we repay the Lord for all that he has repaid us?"
And see that it is not even said, "which he has given us,"
but "which he has repaid us," by that generous bestower, as if the beginning of that grace had not been his doing, but his good gift were a repayment for things done earlier.
For he counts the thanksgiving of those who receive as a good deed [?] done to him,

he who gives you what you need and then asks mercy from you by way of [?] the poor; and if he receives back from you in full what is his own, he gives you thanks for it, as if you had given it from what is yours.
"What then shall we repay the Lord for all that he has repaid us?" For I do not depart from that voice of the prophet,
who is rightly astonished and looks around at his own poverty, seeing that he has nothing worthy to repay that King,
who, in addition to so many and such great and splendid benefactions, which have no number, nor end, nor measure, which he has done for us,
promises us, greater and more manifold than all of them, the gifts to be given at the last: the delight of paradise, the glory of the kingdom, honor equal to the angels, and the vision of God,
which for those made worthy is the highest of all good things, that vision of him for which every rational nature longs,
of which may we too be made worthy, once we have purified ourselves from the passions of the flesh through Christ Jesus,
our good King and Lord, to whom belong glory and might forever and ever. Amen.
Now someone will say to us: "And how shall we maintain fellowship and love toward our brothers, which is the head of all good things and the most perfect of all,
for the end of the law is love? And how shall we show it to our neighbors when we go in to visit people
who are in the grip of great trials, if we do not weep with them or shed tears, but give thanks to God for what has befallen them?
For to bear one's own affliction with thanksgiving is a sign of patience, but to give thanks to God over a neighbor's trials is a form of rejoicing over evil.
And who would wish to be distressed more than the distressed person himself? For the apostle commands us this too: to weep with those who weep. What then shall we say to all this?
But it is good that I should remind you once more of the words of the Lord, as to the matters over which rejoicing is commanded and those over which grief is commanded.
For he says: "Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven," and again he says:
"Do not weep for me, but weep for your children."
So then the divine word teaches us rejoicing and gladness with the righteous, and again, with those who have come to repentance and shed tears,
that we should mourn and lament with them; or else, for those who are without remorse over their sins, that we should weep for them too, for they do not know how they are perishing.

But he does not command us in this way, that we should weep over a person's death and cry aloud together with the mourners, and so suppose that in this manner we are fulfilling the apostle's commandments.
For neither do I praise the physician who, instead of healing the sick person, himself also contracts that person's disease;
nor the helmsman who, instead of strengthening those on board, instead of fighting the winds, instead of devising means against the waves,
and instead of comforting the fearful, cuts off hope, is afraid and goes to pieces like people with no experience of the sea.
For such is the person who goes in to mourners and does not give them a word of benefit, but rather himself also becomes a sharer in the unseemliness of the passions of others.
To be sorrowful, then, over the trials of the mourners is fitting, so that in this way one may show one's kinship with their grief,
so as not to be cheerful over their trials, nor to take pleasure in the sorrow of others.
But to lament with them beyond measure is improper: to cry out and weep aloud with the sufferer, and to imitate the other actions of one who is darkened by passion,
that is, to tear one's garment along with him. Shutting oneself up in darkness,
putting on black clothing, rolling in ashes, and leaving the hair unshorn: for through these actions the trial is made to grow all the more, rather than to subside.
Do you not see that numbings [?] and pains of the spleen and liver are added?
The one on [?] and the other make wounds and pains all the stronger, whereas hands soothe aching limbs by gentle touch and kneading.
So you too, then, do not inflame the passion by your coming, and do not fall down along with the one who has fallen.
For the one who would raise up a person who has fallen must surely be higher than the fallen one, but whoever has fallen along with him himself needs another to raise him up.
Rather, one ought to feel pain of heart over the trial that has come upon one's neighbor, and to grieve quietly over the matter
by changing the appearance of the face to sadness and with a seemly gravity that shows the grief of the soul.
And when you begin to speak, it is not good to come at once with reproach upon the afflicted person, for reproach is heavy to a soul
embittered by sorrow, and harsh words spoken by those who stand outside the suffering
are not accepted by such people and are useless for consolation. Instead, one should let them be,
so that they may cry out and lament, vainly and without profit; and when the evil has subsided a little and grown milder, then begin to console them gently and sweetly.
For the trainers of colts too, when they see a fierce and wild colt, do not immediately choke it with the bridle,
nor do they pull hard on the bridle all at once, for in this way it grows all the more violent and carries off the one sitting on it.
Instead, they first leave it to its own will and go along with it, and when they see that its anger has been calmed by its own violence and running,
then they begin to train it, and by skill they bring it to obedience.
So it will be according to the saying of Solomon: "It is good to go into the house of mourning rather than into the house of drinking,"

provided only that one strives to use speech with skill and gentleness, and so to impart his own health to the sick person as well, and that he not take that other person's disorderly wailing into himself, like blindness.
This, then, is weeping with those who weep: that when you see a brother who has fallen into sin and has come to repentance and is weeping,
you weep with him and lament and have pity and suffer with him, for in this way the healing of your own passions will come about for you through the passions of another.
For whoever sheds hot tears for the sin of his neighbor also heals himself, since he is mourning for a brother.
Such was the one who said: "Anguish has seized me because of the sinners who have forsaken your law."
Weep for sin, for another's as well, and all the more for your own.
This is the sickness of the soul, this is the death of that which is immortal, this is what deserves mourning and unceasing lament.
Over this let every tear flow, and let the sighing that rises from the depths of the heart never cease.
For Paul wept over those enemies of the cross of Christ, and Jeremiah wept over the destruction of the people,
who, since natural tears were not enough for him, therefore asked for a fountain of tears and for the utmost measure:
"And I will sit and weep day and night for this people, who are perishing."
Such tears and such mourning the word calls blessed, and not that of the person who is easily overwhelmed by every sorrow and is seized by wailing for every reason.
And again I have seen some of the lovers of pleasure who, from the excess of their desires and on account of their love, under the pretext of grief, for enjoyment
and they turn aside to drunkenness, and they want to console their dissoluteness with the words of Solomon, who says: "Give wine to the sorrowful."
But that saying of the "Proverbs" does not counsel drunkenness; rather, it lays down a rule for human life.
For, to leave aside its figurative sense, in which it calls rational joy wine, not even the plain force of the saying is to be despised,
for, so that those who mourn grievously may not be swallowed up by their great sorrow and disdain even the taking of food,
but rather so that the heart of those given to mourning may be strengthened with bread, and its fallen strength may be fortified with wine, for this reason it was said.
But those lovers of wine and seekers of drunkenness do not engage in that heavy drinking to calm their sorrow;
rather, they exchange evil for evil and become wicked merchants, for they purchase a sickness of the soul with yet another sickness.
They resemble a tilting balance that never comes level: in the same way, these people take away from their sorrow only as much as they increase their love of pleasure.
Rather, wine should be taken as a help to nature, and not in such a way that the mind is darkened,
for in that way sorrow departs along with the wine, and the evil of drunkenness comes upon the soul.
For if the mind is the physician of sorrow, then drunkenness is the worst of evils, for it destroys that healing of the soul.
But understand well each of these things that have been said, and you will find how the teaching of the Apostle is both possible and profitable:
how one must rejoice always, in the true sense of the word, and how you may pray without ceasing, and how you may give thanks in everything, and in what manner you may console the sorrowful,
so that you may be perfect in every respect and established by the help of the Holy Spirit and by the coming of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,
to whom belong glory and power, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
